prize_parts.citation: For showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting shape the pattern and welfare gains of international trade.

statement.case_for: B020 is a theory built to be taken to data, which is the kind of contribution I weight most. Melitz (2003) moved the unit of analysis from the industry to the firm. It gave a tractable account of who exports, who exits and how openness reallocates resources toward more productive firms. That produced testable predictions that firm-level datasets could confront directly. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) added the exporting-versus-FDI margin, so the framework reached multinational activity, not only exporting. The work has run for over twenty years. It is the standard foundation for empirical trade, and it spilled into industrial organisation and macro through quantitative models. It is mature, widely replicated and policy-relevant for evaluating trade agreements. Attribution is also workable: a Melitz-Helpman pairing identifies the model and its first major extension, and does not stretch credit across a large team. Trade was last honoured in 2008 for the new trade theory and economic geography. Firm heterogeneity is a distinct advance that builds on that work and does not repeat it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and framing. Several colleagues note that the empirical firm-level foundations by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on the credited list. A two-name award could therefore leave out people with a reasonable claim to co-origination. Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions are real, and a three-name version is defensible. Helpman is also the common name in B001, so the Committee would have to decide which of his bodies of work it is honouring. Some of the welfare-gains results depend on parametric assumptions, such as Pareto productivity and CES demand. Krugman's 2008 recognition also leaves some overlap in framing.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B020 first. He sees Melitz as the clear core and Helpman as a natural partner. He flags that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on the ballot entry, and that Helpman's other candidacy in B001 might lead the Committee to combine or split his credit.
responses.response: I agree on the core and share the concern about the credit boundary. Because those names are absent from the credited list, I cannot responsibly add them to a configuration. My view is that the Committee should decide the boundary in the citation wording. A phrasing centred on firm heterogeneity and selection in the Melitz-Helpman framework is accurate about what is credited, and it does not claim the empirical firm-level literature is exhausted. I disagree mildly that Redding is only an extension. If the Committee wants a prize that reaches quantitative practice, a third name is arguable, but I prefer the narrower award because the conceptual step is clearer.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B020 first and describes Melitz as the workhorse model. He treats Redding as later and more derivative. He notes the attribution gap from the empirical pioneers, and the overlap with Helpman in B001.
responses.response: I accept his framing, including the gap he identifies. Where I would qualify it is on the Helpman overlap. I do not think B020 and B001 compete in a way that should lower B020. They are different achievements, and each stands on its own merits. For a single prize, the better test is which contribution has more empirical content and wider spillover across fields. On that test I think B020 has the edge. That is a judgment about spillover, and it does not mean B001 is any less rigorous.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first. He argues that Grossman and Helpman provide the canonical framework for how organised interests shape trade policy, that the attribution is a clean pair, and that the work has been mature for decades.
responses.response: The cleanliness of the pair and the maturity are not in doubt, and I rank B001 among my alternatives for that reason. My reservation is the empirical record. Teorell concedes that support for protection-for-sale predictions is mixed in some applications. Several colleagues agree, including Andersson and Krusell. For me, a theory whose influence runs ahead of its confirmation counts for less than a framework that went on to organise firm-level evidence. I do not claim B001 is unworthy. Reasonable members can weigh theoretical depth against empirical traction differently, and I would not treat the gap as decisive.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B016 first, B001 second and B031 third. For B031 he proposes adding Gertler to Kiyotaki and Moore, and he notes that Bernanke's 2022 prize partly covered related ground.
responses.response: I rank B031 as a strong alternative, and I agree the overlap with 2022 is the main issue. I would still keep the award to Kiyotaki and Moore. Their 1997 paper is the identifiable origin of the collateral-amplification mechanism. Adding Gertler would pull in the Bernanke-Gertler financial-accelerator line, where a prior laureate shares the credit. That would blur the citation. Where I differ from Krusell is that I give B031 less weight than B020 because its empirical identification is more indirect. I do not say that to dispute its importance for macro-finance and post-2008 policy.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would want to credit Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as co-originators. They are not on the credited list, so I cannot place them in a configuration.
Whether Redding belongs in a third seat, or whether the Melitz-Helpman pair is the cleaner attribution.
How robust the welfare-gains results are to parametric assumptions, and how much that should count against the empirical side of the case.
Whether the Committee prefers to recognise Helpman for B001, B020 or both. I have not worked out whether a split configuration is feasible under the three-person limit.
My assessments of priority and attribution come from recollection and the supplied evidence, and I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in corporate finance, venture capital and private equity, with no connection to the trade candidates or their credited names. The profile lists long committee overlap with several colleagues, but that is not a candidate-specific connection.
